failures.title: Porsche MA1.76 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Wastegate Actuator Failure - 991.2 twin-turbo units
items.whatHappens: The wastegate actuators on the 991.2 twin-turbo MA1.76 are a known weak point. Road salt and corrosion can damage the actuator mechanism, leading to underboosting, engine fault warnings, and reduced performance. The car may trigger a fault light without a check engine light (CEL) - diagnosis requires a Porsche diagnostic scanner.
items.repairVsReplace: Wastegate actuators can be replaced individually without replacing the entire turbocharger. However, Porsche Technical often recommends replacing both turbos and associated ancillaries if the failure is corrosion-related. This is a significant repair (£2,000-£4,000 at an independent specialist) but far cheaper than a full engine replacement. Read our full turbocharger failure guide

items.title: Water Pump Failure
items.whatHappens: Water pump failure is well-documented on the 991.2 MA1.76. Symptoms include sudden overheating during normal driving, with coolant temperatures spiking to 250°F+ and oil temperatures exceeding 240°F. The water pump may be found weeping upon inspection.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump replacement is a routine but labour-intensive repair (£800-£1,500 at an independent specialist). If overheating has occurred, cylinder head inspection and potential gasket replacement may be required - costs escalate significantly.

items.title: Ignition Coil and Sensor Failures
items.whatHappens: Ignition coil packs can fail without warning, triggering misfires and rough running. Crankshaft position sensors sometimes fail when the engine gets hot, causing the car to stall or cut out at low RPM. These are common on higher-mileage 991.2 units.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil packs and sensors are relatively inexpensive parts (£200-£500 each) with moderate labour costs. Proactive replacement is recommended on higher-mileage cars.

failures.goodYearsLine: The MA1.76 3.0L twin-turbo is considered more robust than the naturally aspirated 3.8L it replaced, with no IMS bearing issues or bore scoring concerns. Wastegate and water pump failures are the primary documented weaknesses - both are repairable without engine replacement.

variants.title: MA1.76 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The MA1.76 code covers two fundamentally different engine families - this is the single most important distinction for anyone buying a replacement. - Fitted to: 991.2 911 Carrera, Carrera S, Carrera 4, Carrera 4S, Targa 4, Targa 4S (2016-2019) - Key technical difference: 2,981 cc displacement, twin-turbocharged, 370-420 hp output. Direct injection with Bosch MED17 ECU. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Wastegate actuator failure and water pump failure are documented on this variant. - Interchange note: Not interchangeable with the 4.0L MA1.76 - displacement, induction, ECU calibration, and engine mounts all differ. - Fitted to: 991.1 GT3 RS (2015-2017) - Key technical difference: 3,996 cc displacement, naturally aspirated, 500 hp / 373 kW output. High-revving motorsport-derived engine with 9,000 rpm redline. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the MA1.76 code but is a completely different engine family - different failure patterns apply (finger follower DLC coating wear, oiling issues on early units). - Interchange note: Absolutely not interchangeable with the 3.0L twin-turbo MA1.76 - this is a completely different engine with different mounting points, ECU, cooling, and exhaust systems. - Fitted to: 991.2 GT3 (2017-2019) - Key technical difference: 4.0L naturally aspirated, 500 hp / 368 kW output. Updated from the 991.1 GT3 RS unit with revised DLC coating on finger rockers. - Sub-code-specific failure note: More robust than the 991.1 GT3 RS unit; the DLC coating was revised to address wear issues. - Interchange note: Shares the MA1.76 code but is a different engine from the 3.0L twin-turbo - confirm displacement before ordering.

relatives.description: the 3.8L flat-six that powered the 991.1 Carrera S. The MA1.76 replaced it with twin-turbocharging, delivering more torque and better responsiveness, though some purists miss the naturally aspirated character.

4.0L naturally aspirated (991.1 GT3 RS, 991.2 GT3) - critically, the MA1.76 code is also used for the 4.0L naturally aspirated engine in GT3 and GT3 RS models. This is a completely different engine - if you have a GT3, you are looking at the 4.0L unit, not the 3.0L twin-turbo covered here.
a higher-output variant of the 3.0L twin-turbo engine, producing 450 hp in the Carrera 4 GTS and 911 T. It shares the MA1.75 code and is closely related to the MA1.76.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement MA1.76 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used MA1.76 3.0L twin-turbo can make sense for a 991.2 owner facing an out-of-warranty failure, but only if the engine comes with documented service history and - critically - proof that the wastegate actuators and water pump have been addressed. The primary risk is hidden turbo damage from wastegate failure or overheating from water pump failure.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper MA1.76 recon addresses the engine's specific failure points: wastegate actuator inspection/replacement, full water pump and cooling system overhaul, and replacement of all gaskets and seals. This is the right call for a high-value 991.2 where the car's value justifies the spend - a £55,000-£90,000 991.2 Carrera S comfortably absorbs a £16,500-£22,000 replacement.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for the MA1.76 when the engine has suffered catastrophic failure (turbo failure, overheating damage) and the original block is still viable. For the 4.0L naturally aspirated MA1.76 (GT3/GT3 RS), rebuilds are more common due to the motorsport nature of these engines - upgraded internals can address finger follower wear and oiling concerns.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** Fitting through the EnginesMarket network ensures your replacement MA1.76 is supplied by a vetted Porsche specialist with a minimum 12-month warranty. Supply-only or full supply & fit available nationwide.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The MA1.76 3.0L twin-turbo is fitted to 991.2-generation 911s, which hold £45,000-£90,000 depending on spec and mileage. A £16,500-£22,000 replacement engine is a significant but generally justifiable expense relative to the vehicle's value. For the 4.0L MA1.76 (991.1 GT3 RS / 991.2 GT3), values are £80,000-£150,000+, making replacement more easily justifiable. For a high-mileage 991.2 Carrera at the lower end of the value spectrum (£40,000-£50,000), evaluate the car's overall condition and service history before committing - a used engine may be more cost-effective.

items.question: What are the common problems with the MA1.76 engine?
items.answer: The most significant known issues are wastegate actuator failure (20k-50k miles) and water pump failure (20k-50k miles). Wastegate actuator failure leads to underboosting and reduced performance, while water pump failure can cause sudden overheating. Ignition coil and sensor failures are also reported on higher-mileage units. Wastegate failure is often caused by road salt corrosion - replacing the actuator alone may not be sufficient if corrosion has spread. Water pump failure can cause overheating and potential cylinder head damage if not addressed promptly. The MA1.76 3.0L twin-turbo is considered more robust than the naturally aspirated 3.8L it replaced, with no IMS bearing issues.

The same code is also used for the 4.0L naturally aspirated engine in the 991.1 GT3 RS and 991.2 GT3 - these are completely different engines. The 3.0L twin-turbo MA1.76 is the most common version, powering the base Carrera and Carrera S. The 4.0L MA1.76 is a high-revving motorsport-derived engine exclusive to GT3 and GT3 RS models. items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt MA1.76?
items.answer: A used MA1.76 can be viable if it has full service history and documented wastegate/water pump replacement - but the risk of hidden turbo damage is real. Reconditioned is the safest option for a high-value 991.2, as it addresses all known failure points (wastegate actuators, water pump, gaskets). A full rebuild is justified if your original block is still sound and you want upgraded internals for track use or if you have a GT3 RS unit where rebuilds are more common. For a 991.2 Carrera with lower value, a used engine may be more cost-effective. Always insist on a warranty of at least 12 months for any replacement.

items.question: How do I confirm my car has the MA1.76 engine and not another variant?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on the engine block and appears on your V5C registration document. The most reliable way to confirm is via Porsche VIN decoder - the 8th character of the VIN indicates engine type. Critical: the MA1.76 code covers both the 3.0L twin-turbo (991.2 Carrera) AND the 4.0L naturally aspirated (991.1 GT3 RS, 991.2 GT3) - confirm displacement before proceeding. The 3.0L twin-turbo MA1.76 has 2,981 cc displacement and is fitted to 991.2 Carrera models. The 4.0L MA1.76 has 3,996 cc displacement and is fitted to 991.1 GT3 RS and 991.2 GT3.

items.question: How long do MA1.76 engines typically last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance, an MA1.76 3.0L twin-turbo can exceed 100,000 miles. However, turbocharged engines require diligent oil changes and cooling system maintenance. The biggest longevity factors are oil condition and cooling system health - regular oil changes (every 6,000-8,000 miles or annually) and water pump servicing are critical. Wastegate actuator and water pump failures are the primary wear items - addressing them preventatively can extend engine life. The 4.0L naturally aspirated MA1.76 (GT3/GT3 RS) is more demanding on maintenance due to its high-revving nature. Regular Porsche specialist inspection is recommended from 40,000 miles.
